title: ISAs, Operating Systems, and Virtual Memory
summary: This unit compares x86, RISC-V, and ARM in terms of registers, calling conventions (Aufrufkonventionen), addressing modes (Adressierungsarten), and instruction formats (Befehlsformen). It then covers multiuser systems (Mehrbenutzersysteme), interrupts, and virtual memory (virtueller Speicher), including address translation with page tables (Seitentabellen), the TLB, and paging.
keyFacts: x86 is a CISC instruction set architecture (Befehlssatzarchitektur) with many complex instructions, variable instruction lengths, and support for legacy execution modes.
IA-32 refers to the 32-bit version; x86_64, also called Intel 64, is a later 64-bit extension that originally came from AMD.
The same x86 registers can be accessed as RAX (64 bits), EAX (32 bits), AX (16 bits), or AH/AL (8 bits each).

In the x86_64 calling convention shown, the first six parameters are passed in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, and r9, in that order; additional parameters are passed on the stack. The return value is in rax.
In IA-32, call places the return address on the stack; in RISC-V, jal typically stores the return address in ra.
With base-relative addressing, the effective address is the register contents plus the offset; with scaled indexing, it is the base plus the index multiplied by the operand size.
In the 2-operand form, the destination is also a source. In the 3-operand register-register form, the two sources and the destination are separate.
ARMv8 (AArch64) is ARM's first 64-bit ISA. The similarities with RISC-V described here include RISC, 4-byte instructions, and load/store.
Time sharing saves the state of an interrupted program, lets the scheduler select the next program, and loads that program's state.
Interrupts are asynchronous and triggered by external events; exceptions are synchronous and associated with an executed instruction.
The MMU translates virtual addresses into physical addresses during memory accesses; virtual pages can be mapped to noncontiguous physical frames.
With 4-KiB pages, the offset is 12 bits and remains unchanged during translation.
An Sv32 page-table entry includes V, R/W/X, U, G, A, and D, among other fields. Invalid entries or impermissible accesses cause an exception.
In the X/W/R bit patterns, 001, 011, 100, 101, and 111 mean read, read/write, execute, read/execute, and read/write/execute, respectively; 010 and 110 are reserved.
Multilevel page tables avoid having to reserve entries in a large single-level table for unused regions of the virtual address space.
A TLB caches recently used address translations; without a TLB, Sv39 requires three page-table accesses before the actual data access.
With lazy allocation, a virtual page receives a physical frame only after an access triggers an exception.
With paging, a selected page is marked as not present and swapped out; a later access triggers it to be brought back in. Pinned pages are not swapped out.

review.notes: 45 Fragen geprüft. Präzisiert: die Sv39-Frage zum TLB-Miss, die Bedeutung von U und X/W/R sowie die Byte-Reihenfolge bei Little Endian. Alle Rechenprüfungen und Antwortmengen stimmen; jedes Level hat mindestens 8 Fragen.

questions.prompt: Which description applies to x86?

options.text: A CISC ISA with complex instructions and variable instruction lengths
An ISA containing only floating-point instructions
A RISC ISA with instructions that are all 4 bytes long
An ISA with only one execution mode and no legacy modes

questions.explanation: x86 is described as a CISC ISA with many complex instructions, variable instruction lengths, and support for legacy modes.

questions.prompt: What is the word size of x86_64, also called Intel 64?

options.text: 128 bits
32 bits
16 bits
64 bits

questions.explanation: x86_64, also called Intel 64, is the 64-bit extension of the x86 family.

questions.prompt: Which descriptions of x86 extensions are correct? Select all correct statements.

options.text: Transactional Memory is associated with speculative execution and atomic accesses.
F16C converts half-precision floating-point values.
F16C is the extension for additional stack registers.
VMX supports virtual machines.
VMX performs virtual-to-physical address translation in the MMU.

questions.explanation: VMX, F16C, and Transactional Memory are associated with the purposes given in a, b, and c, respectively. The other descriptions are not associated with these extensions.

questions.prompt: The 64-bit view of an x86 register is called `RAX`, the 32-bit view `EAX`, the 16-bit view `AX`, and the 8-bit subregister views `AH` and `___`.

options.text: AL
EAX
R8
BL

questions.explanation: AH and AL are the two 8-bit subregister views of the AX register.

questions.prompt: Where does `call` place the return address under the IA-32 calling convention described?

options.text: In register `ra`
On the stack
In register `eax`
In a TLB entry

questions.explanation: In the IA-32 call shown, `call` places the return address on the stack. `ra` is the RISC-V convention being contrasted here.

questions.prompt: For this question, consider only the following x86_64 calling convention: The first six parameters are passed, in order, in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, and `r9`; additional parameters are passed on the stack. The return value is in `rax`. Which statements are correct? Select all correct statements.

options.text: The return value is in `rax`.
The first six parameters are in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, and `r9`.
The seventh and every subsequent parameter is on the stack.
All parameters must be on the stack.
The return value is in `eax`, including in x86_64.

questions.explanation: Under the convention specified in the question, the first six parameters are passed in the listed registers and additional parameters are passed on the stack. The return value is in `rax`.

questions.prompt: With base-relative addressing: effective address = register contents + ___.

options.text: Operand size
Offset
Page number
Return address

questions.explanation: The offset is added to the base register address to obtain the effective address.

questions.prompt: RISC-V supports direct addressing, in which the memory address itself appears in the instruction.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The table marks direct addressing as "no" for RISC-V; register-indirect and displacement addressing are supported.

questions.prompt: What does `add edx, eax` do in the x86 2-operand form described?

options.text: `eax = edx + eax`
The value from `edx` is written to memory.
`edx = edx + eax`
`edx = eax`

questions.explanation: In this 2-operand form, the first operand is both the destination and a source; the result overwrites `edx`.

questions.prompt: After which step does Program B resume execution?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  A["Interrupt Program A"] --> S["Save state"]
  S --> P["Scheduler selects program"]
  P --> L["Load B's state"]
  L --> B["Resume Program B"]
context.caption: Simplified time-sharing process

options.text: Only after Program A has finished
Immediately after Program A is interrupted, without a context switch
After the scheduler selects Program B and loads its state
Before Program A's state is saved

questions.explanation: The process first saves A's state, then selects B and loads B's state before resuming B.

questions.prompt: What does the MMU do in the virtual memory system described?

options.text: It determines the order of a compiler's instructions.
It stores all return addresses for a process.
It translates virtual addresses into physical addresses.
It selects the next program for the scheduler.

questions.explanation: The MMU performs address translation in hardware during memory accesses; the operating system controls the mapping.

questions.prompt: An instruction uses the base-relative addressing rule `EA = Registerinhalt + Offset`. With register contents `0x1000` and offset `0x18`, what effective address results?

options.text: 0x0FE8

questions.explanation: `0x1000 + 0x18 = 0x1018`. The offset is added to the base.

questions.prompt: With scaled indexing, `EA = Basis + Index × Operandenlänge`. Given base `0x2000`, index `3`, and operand size `4` bytes, what effective address results?
questions.explanation: The index contribution is `3 × 4 = 12 = 0xC`; therefore, `EA = 0x2000 + 0xC = 0x200C`.

questions.prompt: An IA-32 stack frame uses `ebp` as its reference point. According to the layout, what is at `[ebp+8]`?

options.text: The return address
Parameter 2
Parameter 1
A local variable

questions.explanation: In the layout shown, Parameter 1 is at `[ebp+8]`, Parameter 2 is at `[ebp+12]`, and the return address is at `[ebp+4]`.

questions.prompt: A program executes `c += i` and wants to update `c` in memory. Which statements about the ISA examples shown are correct? Select all correct statements.

options.text: With `add edx, eax`, the result is stored in a new third register.
With `add DWORD PTR [ebp-0x10], eax`, x86 can perform arithmetic directly in memory.
RISC-V performs the same memory operation directly with a single `add` instruction.
RISC-V typically needs `lw`, `add`, and `sw` for this.

questions.explanation: The x86 example allows addition directly at a memory location. RISC-V uses a load, computation in a register, and a store; `add edx, eax` also overwrites the first operand.

questions.prompt: A loop starts with `i=0` and `c=0`. In each iteration, it adds `i` to `c`, increments `i` by 1, and continues as long as the new value satisfies `i ≤ 9`. What is the final value of `c`?
questions.explanation: The loop adds the values from 0 through 9, inclusive. Their sum is 45; checking after the increment makes the loop stop at `i=10`.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of `add [ebp-0x10], eax` in the x86 code shown?

options.text: The memory contents are copied to `eax` without addition.
The instruction compares the memory contents with `eax` and sets flags.
The value of `eax` is added to the memory contents at `[ebp-0x10]`; the result remains there.
The value of `eax` is appended to the address `[ebp-0x10]`.

questions.explanation: The instruction shown operates directly on memory: it increments the memory value by `eax` and overwrites that value in place.

questions.prompt: In RISC-V `Vectored` mode, asynchronous interrupts use `Einsprungadresse = BASE + 4 × cause`. Given `BASE = 0x1000` and `cause = 7`, what trap entry address results?
questions.explanation: `4 × 7 = 28 = 0x1C`; adding it to `0x1000` gives `0x101C`.

questions.prompt: In X/W/R order, the pattern `101` means: read and ___.

options.text: A pointer to the next table level
write only
execute
write

questions.explanation: `101` sets X and R: the page is executable and readable, but not writable.

questions.prompt: A virtual page is mapped to physical page number `0x12345`. With 4-KiB pages, the offset `0xABC` remains unchanged. What physical address results?

options.text: 0x12345ABC
0x12344ABC
0xABC12345

questions.explanation: The physical page base is `0x12345 × 0x1000 = 0x12345000`. With the unchanged offset `0xABC`, the result is `0x12345ABC`.

questions.prompt: In the translation shown, there is no matching TLB entry. Which step follows in the diagram?

context.content:
flowchart TD
  VA["Virtual address"] --> T{"Translation in TLB?"}
  T -->|Yes| C{"Entry and access valid?"}
  T -->|No| W["Read page tables"]
  W --> C
  C -->|Yes| PA["Physical address"]
  C -->|No| E["Exception"]
  PA --> M["Memory access"]
context.caption: Schematic process for a TLB hit or access fault

options.text: The offset is replaced by the physical page number.
The page tables are read.
The data access happens immediately without translation.
The scheduler selects a different process.

questions.explanation: On a TLB miss, the page tables are read; the entry and access are then checked.

questions.prompt: For this question, use the following RISC-V system-call convention: For a system call using `ecall`, the system-call number is in `a7`; the parameters are passed in `a0` through `a6`. Where are the number and parameters?

options.text: Number in `a0`, parameters in `a1` through `a7`
Number in `sp`, parameters in `t0` through `t6`
Number on the stack, parameters in `ra`
Number in `a7`, parameters in `a0` through `a6`

questions.explanation: Under the convention specified in the question, the number is in `a7` and the parameters are in `a0` through `a6`.

questions.prompt: A single-level Sv32 page table contains `2^20` entries, each 4 bytes. How much memory does it require per process?

options.text: 4 KiB
1 MiB
4 MiB
4 GiB

questions.explanation: `2^20 × 4 Byte = 2^22 Byte`, which is 4 MiB.

questions.prompt: In Sv32, `VA = 0x00403ABC` is split into two 10-bit VPN fields and a 12-bit offset. What is the value of `VPN[1]`?

options.text: 0xABC

questions.explanation: The upper 10 bits of the virtual page number give `VPN[1]=1`; the middle VPN field is 3 and the offset is `0xABC`.

questions.prompt: For `VA = 0x00403ABC`, the page tables provide physical page number `0x12345`. With 4-KiB pages, the offset remains unchanged. What physical address results?

options.text: 0x12344ABC
0x00403ABC
0x12345ABC

questions.explanation: The page number gives the physical base `0x12345000`; the virtual offset `0xABC` is preserved. Together, these give `0x12345ABC`.

questions.prompt: The access bits are ordered X, W, R (execute, write, read). A pattern labeled "reserved" is not a valid access permission and must not be interpreted as a combination of its set individual bits. Which statements about the table are correct? Select all correct statements.

context.content:
| X/W/R | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `000` | Pointer to the next table level |
| `001` | Read only |
| `011` | Read and write |
| `100` | Execute only |
| `101` | Read and execute |
| `111` | Read, write, and execute |
| `010` / `110` | Reserved: not a valid access permission |
context.caption: Meaning of the X/W/R patterns

options.text: `100` allows execute only.
`011` allows read and write.
`000` is a pointer to the next table level.
`110` allows read and write.
`010` means write only.

questions.explanation: In X/W/R order, `011` means read and write, `100` means execute only, and `000` is a pointer to the next table level. `010` and `110` are reserved and therefore are not valid access permissions.

questions.prompt: A process is running in user mode. For this access, `U=1` allows access in user mode, and `U=0` marks a privileged page. The page-table entry is valid, but `U=0`. What happens when the page is accessed?

options.text: The access automatically switches to system mode.
The access proceeds if the TLB hits.
An exception is raised.
The MMU automatically sets `U` to 1.

questions.explanation: A privileged page cannot be used in user mode. A valid entry or a TLB hit does not bypass the access check.

questions.prompt: Sv39 has three page-table levels. Without a TLB, how many page-table accesses are needed for a translation before the actual data access?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

questions.explanation: Sv39 uses three table levels. Without a TLB, this requires three table accesses plus the actual data access.

questions.prompt: A program requests new virtual memory, but initially no physical page is assigned. What happens on the first access?

options.text: The access is permanently discarded because virtual pages cannot be assigned frames.
An exception causes the operating system to find a frame and add the page-table entry.
The scheduler automatically copies the page into the TLB.
The virtual address is used unchanged as the physical address.

questions.explanation: With lazy allocation, the physical page is assigned only on first access. The resulting exception prompts the operating system to find a frame and update the table.

questions.prompt: Physical memory is full and a new page needs to be loaded. Which steps match the paging process described? Select all correct statements.

options.text: The operating system selects a page and marks it as not present.
The selected page is written to disk; its frame can be used for the new page.
A later access to the swapped-out page triggers an exception so that it can be brought back in.
The TLB is used as a disk area for the swapped-out page.
All operating-system pages must be swapped out first.

questions.explanation: With paging, a selected page is swapped out and its frame is reassigned. A later access to the swapped-out page triggers an exception, after which the page can be brought back in.

source.heading: Paging: Auslagern, wenn keine Kachel frei ist

questions.prompt: A valid Sv32 leaf entry at the first level can point directly to a large 4-MiB page.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: In Sv32, a leaf entry at the first level points directly to a large 4-MiB page rather than to another table.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish interrupts from exceptions? Select all correct statements.

options.text: An exception can never be triggered by a deliberate system call.
Interrupts and exceptions are both always synchronous errors from an instruction.
An interrupt is asynchronous and can be triggered by an external event.
A timer event is an example of an interrupt.
An exception is synchronous and associated with an executed instruction.

questions.explanation: Interrupts arise asynchronously from external events such as timers or I/O. Exceptions are synchronous; a deliberate system call is given as a possible example.

questions.prompt: Why are page tables and certain areas of the operating system pinned during the paging process described?

options.text: So that they are not swapped out.
So that the scheduler deletes them at every context switch.
So that they automatically receive identical addresses in all virtual address spaces.
So that the TLB treats them as executable instructions.

questions.explanation: Pinned pages remain in physical memory. Examples include page tables, parts of the operating system, and pages for devices without an MMU.

source.heading: Paging: Auslagern, wenn keine Kachel frei ist

questions.prompt: A program calls a function that in turn calls another function. In RISC-V, `jal ra, ...` stores the return address in `ra`; in IA-32, `call` places it on the stack. What must the RISC-V code account for during a nested call?

options.text: Save the current return address in `ra` before the next `jal` overwrites it.
Copy the return address to `eax` because IA-32 uses `ra`.
Save `ra` because `call` places the address on the stack in RISC-V.
Nothing: `jal` automatically stores every return address in its own register.

questions.explanation: Another `jal` overwrites `ra`, so any return address still needed must be saved first. In IA-32, `call` instead places the return address on the stack.

questions.prompt: A virtual address `0x00403ABC` is mapped to physical page number `0x12345` with a page size of 4 KiB. The offset is preserved during translation. Read four bytes starting at the resulting physical address, in ascending address order. Little-endian order here means that the byte at the lowest address forms bits 7–0, the next byte forms bits 15–8, and so on. What 32-bit value do you get?

context.caption: Bytes in memory in ascending address order

questions.explanation: The offset of the virtual address is `0xABC`. This gives physical address `0x12345 × 0x1000 + 0xABC = 0x12345ABC`. The bytes at this address and the next three addresses are `78 56 34 12`. In little-endian order, they give `0x12345678`.

questions.prompt: An array of 4-byte elements begins at virtual address `0x00403000`. Element 2 is at `Basis + Index × Elementgröße`. The virtual page is mapped to physical page number `0x12345`; the offset is preserved. What is the physical address of Element 2?
questions.explanation: Element 2 is at `0x00403000 + 2 × 4 = 0x00403008`, so its offset is `0x008`. The physical page base is `0x12345000`; therefore, the physical address is `0x12345008`.

questions.prompt: A timer interrupts Program A so the operating system can run Program B. Which statements match the time-sharing process described? Select all correct statements.

options.text: The scheduler selects which program runs next.
B's state does not need to be loaded before B resumes.
The operating system saves A's registers, SP, and PC, among other things.
Program A can switch directly to system mode by executing arbitrary privileged code.
A timer event is an asynchronous interrupt.

questions.explanation: Time sharing saves the state of the interrupted program, lets the scheduler select the next program, and loads that program's state. A timer is an external, asynchronous interrupt event; user code cannot arbitrarily assume privileged rights.

questions.prompt: A process uses Sv32 for only a small part of its virtual address space. Why can multilevel page tables save memory in this case?

options.text: Each process automatically gets larger physical frames.
The TLB permanently replaces the page table.
Unused table regions do not need to be created.
Virtual addresses are shortened to 12 bits.

questions.explanation: Multilevel tables make it possible to create tables only for areas that are actually used. A single-level Sv32 table, by contrast, would use 4 MiB per process.

questions.prompt: An instruction is fetched from a page in user mode. The entry is valid, and `U=1` allows access in user mode. The X/W/R bits mean execute/write/read, in that order; therefore, `101` means execute and read. Is the access allowed?

options.text: No, `101` allows only write and execute.
Yes, the page is readable and executable in user mode.
Yes, but only if the entry is invalid.
No, `U=1` prohibits instruction fetches.

questions.explanation: `101` in X/W/R order means execute and read. With a valid entry and `U=1`, the instruction fetch is allowed in user mode.

questions.prompt: A TLB hit provides a valid translation, but the entry allows reading and prohibits writing. The process attempts a store. What happens?

options.text: The offset is set to zero and the store is retried.
The scheduler automatically sets the write bit.
The store succeeds because the TLB hit.
An exception is raised because the write is not permitted.

questions.explanation: A TLB hit provides the translation but does not override access protection. A write to a read-only page causes an exception.

questions.prompt: Two accesses cause exceptions: Access A reaches a virtual page that has never been physically allocated; Access B reaches a page that was previously swapped out. Which statements correctly distinguish the cases? Select all correct statements.

options.text: Both exceptions can be part of page management.
For A, lazy allocation can assign a frame for the first time.
For B, the MMU is responsible for reading the page from disk by itself.
For B, the operating system can bring the swapped-out page back from disk.
For A, a page must be brought back from disk.

questions.explanation: Lazy allocation assigns a frame to a previously unbacked virtual page on its first access. For an access to a swapped-out page, the operating system must bring the page back; in both cases, the exception can initiate the management process.

questions.prompt: Access protection can be used deliberately to catch, for example, array overflows as exceptions during debugging.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The lecture notes mention deliberately blocking accesses to detect array overflows and underflows during debugging.

questions.prompt: Which comparison of instruction formats is correct?

options.text: In the 3-operand form, the destination must overwrite one of the two sources.
x86 is a 3-operand register-register ISA; RISC-V is a 2-operand memory ISA.
x86 can use the destination as a source in the 2-operand form; RISC-V uses a 3-operand register-register form for `x = y + z`.
Both forms must always store the result directly in memory.

questions.explanation: The x86 register machine described uses the 2-operand form, in which the destination overwrites a source. RISC-V uses the load/store register-register form with separate source and destination operands.

questions.prompt: A RISC-V process returns to user mode after an exception. Which statement correctly describes this controlled transition?

options.text: The return can use a privileged instruction such as `mret` or `sret`.
The return happens when the scheduler clears the TLB and loads `ra`.
The transition is impossible because RISC-V has only one mode.
Any user code can gain arbitrary privileged rights by executing `mret`.

questions.explanation: The transitions between system and user mode described are controlled; `mret` and `sret` are privileged return instructions.

levels.title: In Practice: When Addresses Become Part of Everyday Life

questions.prompt: You start an older 32-bit program on an x86_64 PC. Which ISA feature can enable compatibility?

options.text: x86 instructions are always exactly 4 bytes long.
x86 uses only instructions with three operands.
x86_64 retains legacy execution modes.
All x86 registers have the same width.

questions.explanation: x86_64 supplements older word sizes with additional execution modes. Support for a suitable legacy mode can make it possible to run 32-bit programs.

questions.prompt: A database often accesses the same memory pages. Which hardware feature can reduce unnecessary page-table accesses in this situation?

options.text: The stack pointer points to the program stack.
The scheduler selects the next process.
The swap file stores inactive pages.
The TLB stores recently used address translations.

questions.explanation: The TLB (Translation Look-Aside Buffer) stores recently used virtual-to-physical address translations. On a hit, the page-table search can be skipped.

questions.prompt: A memory page is 4 KiB. How many bytes is that? Use 1 KiB = 1024 bytes.
questions.explanation: One KiB is 1024 bytes. Therefore, a 4-KiB page contains 4 × 1024 = 4096 bytes. Page size also determines how many bits are needed for the offset.

questions.prompt: While you type on your smartphone, other programs keep running. Which two events are examples of external interrupts?

options.text: A hardware timer fires.
A memory access by the program violates a permission.
The running program executes an invalid instruction.
A network packet arrives.

questions.explanation: Interrupts arise asynchronously from external events such as network or timer signals. An invalid instruction and an impermissible memory access are associated with an executed instruction and cause exceptions.

questions.prompt: You reserve a large virtual memory region for a simulation but initially use only a small part of it. How can the operating system avoid immediately providing a physical frame for every page?

options.text: It uses lazy allocation and assigns a frame only on first access.
It stores every virtual address in the TLB permanently.
It disables the MMU for the program.
It immediately swaps all pages to disk.

questions.explanation: With lazy allocation, a virtual page receives a physical frame only after its first access. Accessing a page that has not yet been backed can raise an exception, which the operating system handles.

questions.prompt: A page is 4 KiB. How many address bits are needed for the offset within the page? Use 1 KiB = 1024 bytes.
questions.explanation: 4 KiB is 4 × 1024 = 4096 = 2¹² bytes. Therefore, 12 offset bits are needed; these bits remain unchanged when translating a virtual address to a physical address.

questions.prompt: Physical memory is full. The operating system marks a page that has not been used for a long time as not present and writes it to a storage device. Later, the program accesses it again. Which concept does this describe?

options.text: Register renaming: a register receives a new name.
Paging: the page is brought back when needed.
Time sharing: the scheduler switches processes.
Lazy allocation: the page receives memory for the first time.

questions.explanation: With paging, a selected page can be swapped out and marked as not present. A later access raises an exception so that the operating system can bring the page back in.

source.heading: Paging: Auslagern, wenn keine Kachel frei ist

questions.prompt: A hypothetical system translates a virtual address through three page-table levels without a TLB hit. A data value is then read from memory. How many memory accesses are needed in total? Count one access per table level and one for the data value.
questions.explanation: The three table levels require three memory accesses. The subsequent read of the data value brings the total to four accesses.

questions.prompt: A smartphone app runs without privileged rights and wants to read a file. How can it request an operating-system service in a controlled way?

options.text: By bypassing the TLB and changing the page table itself.
By keeping the processor in system mode permanently.
Through a system call that the operating system can check.
By executing privileged device instructions directly in user mode.

questions.explanation: A system call enables a controlled transition from user mode to the operating system. The operating system can check parameters and permissions before performing the service.

questions.prompt: You are reading x86 assembly. Before the instruction, `eax` contains 7 and `ebx` contains 5. What is true after `add eax, ebx`?

options.text: eax contains 12 afterward.
ebx contains 12 afterward.
eax remains 7; the result is in a new register.
The instruction writes 12 directly to memory.

questions.explanation: In this x86 2-operand form, the destination is also a source: the instruction adds `ebx` to `eax` and overwrites `eax` with 12. In a 3-operand register form, the sources and destination would be separate.
